primary.fact: Uranium salts spontaneously emit penetrating radiation recorded on a photographic plate; it was not X-ray radiation.
Marie Curie described radioactivity as an atomic property, named it, and investigated thorium and new elements with Pierre Curie.

primary.locator: Ra table, atomic number and isotope226 row
primary.fact: Ra atomic number88; isotope mass number226 is distinct from its relative atomic mass.
Brackets identify an isotope mass number for elements without a characteristic natural isotopic abundance.

primary.locator: Experimental detection of alpha-particles from the radioactive decay of natural bismuth, abstract
primary.fact: Experimental detection established that natural bismuth is radioactive, rather than a stable exception at atomic number83.

clarifications: Unknown initial radiation is not preidentified as alpha; the observed alpha token remains in a qualified explanation.
Afterglow description replaces the unusual archival term only in modern prose.
Same-condition uranium quantity comparison is distinguished from a universal chemistry-independent intensity claim.
Identification of polonium is not confused with isolating a macroscopic pure sample; Marie Curie receives naming credit.
Bracketed226 is an isotope mass-number convention, not an exact average atomic mass.
No stable isotopes from atomic number83 upward; lower-numbered radioactive isotopes are not excluded.
